name: Adam Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything's confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and also what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Long Acre, which is a co-operative farm, so the twelve of us who work it also own it together. We've got about eighty pigs, a small beef herd, a few fields of barley, an orchard and two acres of vegetables for the box scheme. I start at seven with the pigs, then it's whatever the rota says: weeding leeks, mending fences, loading veg boxes for the van.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two and a half years. Before that I did twenty years at a supermarket warehouse, picking and loading. In 2022 they brought in robot shelving, the kind that drives the racks to you, and I took the redundancy at 54 rather than wait to be pushed. So I'm the new boy here, still learning how to tell a sick pig from a sulky one.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that we decide things together at the Monday meeting, and I like the pigs, they're cleverer than people think. What wears me out is the weeding, bent over for hours. I use AI every day, honestly; I ask it about pig illnesses, I get it to plan my veg rows, and Neil, my partner, laughs that I talk to my phone more than him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, there you go, it was a fancy search engine after all, and the bosses who sacked people for it look silly. At the Monday meeting I'd say we keep doing what we do. Online I'd probably post something cheeky about the warehouse robots that never quite worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit disappointed. I like the stuff, and I'd hoped it would help with the boring parts like the box-scheme orders and the pig records. But for my job and my pay, nothing changes, and the co-op's been steady for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the rota and keep using the AI for the little things, the planting plans and the pig questions. I'd probably offer to set up the box-scheme orders on a simple AI tool so Priya stops doing them by hand on Sunday nights. That's it really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, because I like new things. But I'm secure, Neil's job at the hospital is secure, and we've got four or five months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you took the redundancy from the warehouse. Does that still shape how you see this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. The robot shelving was supposed to be the future, and half the time it broke down and they called the old pickers back on overtime. At the warehouse I learned that the machines are oversold and the people get undersold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your last working years at Long Acre to look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pigs, the orchard, and being properly good at something. I'd like to be the person who knows the pigs best by the time I'm 65. And I'd like to stop the weeding, if my back has a vote.

say: AI turned out to be a **fancy search engine**, and the bosses who sacked people for it look silly.
At the co-op's **Monday meeting** I'd say we carry on doing what we do.
think: I'd be **a bit disappointed**, because I hoped AI would take the boring orders and pig records.
My **job and pay** stay the same, and the co-op has been steady for years.
do: Carry on with the **rota** and keep using AI for planting plans and pig questions.
Set up the **box-scheme orders** on a simple AI tool so Priya stops doing them on Sundays.
feel: **Calm** and secure, if a little flat because I enjoy new things.
S0.quote: At the warehouse I learned that the machines are oversold and the people get undersold.
fieldNote: He is the rare **junior farmhand** who uses AI daily and wants more of it.
Redundancy from the **robot warehouse** made him sceptical of hype but not of the tools.
Co-op ownership and **Neil's hospital job** give him a strong sense of security.

steps.text: Carry on with the pig and veg rota at Long Acre
Set up the box-scheme orders on a simple AI tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the chance for co-ops and workers to own the tools, not just the big firms. At the Monday meeting I'd push for us to try the weeding robots the agricultural college is testing. Online I'd tell people not to be scared but to get organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm well placed. The thinking jobs at Long Acre, the orders, the books, the planning, go to AI first, and I'm already the one who uses it. The hands-on stuff, which is most of my day, changes slowly, so I've got time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd sign up for the college's evening course on farm robots and drones. I'd offer to run a trial of a weeding robot on the veg plot, and set up the AI for the orders and pig records. And I'd keep an eye on the warehouse lads I know, because they'll get hit before us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited even. I know that's not how most people my age feel. But I've been on the losing side of a robot once, and this time I'd like to be the one holding the controller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anyone at Long Acre lose hours if the weeding robot worked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the summer volunteers and maybe Jonah, who mostly weeds. At a co-op we'd vote on it, and I'd argue we move Jonah onto the pigs with me rather than drop him. If it means more people out of work, I'd vote against it, I mean that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're at the junior end. Would the others trust you to run a robot trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would roll their eyes. Priya would back me, because she's sick of the Sunday orders. I'd have to prove it on one bed of leeks first, not the whole two acres.

say: This is the chance for **co-ops and workers** to own the tools, not only big firms.
Don't be scared; **get organised**, and let the co-op try the college's weeding robots.
think: I'm **well placed**, because the co-op's orders and planning go to AI first and I already use it.
Most of my day is **hands-on**, which changes slowly, so I have time to adjust.
do: Sign up this winter for the college's **evening course** on farm robots and drones.
Run a **weeding robot trial** on one bed of leeks before the whole veg plot.
Set up AI for the **orders and pig records**, taking the Sunday work off Priya.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **excited**, which I know is unusual at my age.
S1.quote: I've been on the losing side of a robot once, and this time I'd like to be the one holding the controller.
fieldNote: His warehouse loss turns into **motivation** rather than fear.
He ties automation to **co-op votes** and would oppose it if it cost jobs.
As a junior he knows he must **prove it small** before the others trust him.

steps.text: Sign up for the college's evening course on farm robots
Trial a weeding robot on one bed of leeks
Move the box-scheme orders and pig records onto an AI tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone to plan, and the profits from the robots have to be shared, through taxes or through ownership like ours. At the Monday meeting I'd say we need to decide now what we do in 2031. Online I'd be loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me more than I'd say out loud. By 2028 the planning and the selling are done by AI, fine, I'd welcome that. But by 2031 a robot can feed pigs and pick apples, and I'm 63 with three years' experience, so even in a co-op my hours shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd do the robot maintenance course, so I'm the person who fixes them rather than the one they replace. I'd push the co-op to vote now on sharing out hours fairly when the robots come, so nobody gets dropped. And I'd put an extra hundred and fifty a month away, because a cut in hours is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited about the machines, frightened about the money. It's a strange mix, like waiting for a scan result while reading about a new medicine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would sharing out hours mean for your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If twelve of us at the co-op share the work of six, everyone's on half pay. Half my pay plus Neil's wage keeps the house, just about, but the holidays and the car go. I'd rather that than see Jonah or Mel out on their ear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Those three years between the AI and the robots, what would you do with them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the robots inside out, every bolt. And I'd go round other farms and ask what they're doing, because co-ops that plan together can buy machines together. If we can own the robots, we keep the money in the village.

say: This is **too fast** to plan for, and robot profits must be shared through taxes or ownership.
The co-op must decide **now** what it does when robots arrive in 2031.
think: By **2031** robots can feed pigs and pick apples, so even in a co-op my hours shrink.
At 63 with only three years' experience, I'm **not the one** they need most.
do: Take the **robot maintenance course** straight away, so I fix the machines rather than get replaced.
Push the co-op to vote now on **sharing hours** fairly once robots arrive.
Put an extra **150 a month** away before the cut in hours comes.
feel: **Anxious**, excited about the machines but **frightened** about the money.
S2.quote: If twelve of us at the co-op share the work of six, everyone's on half pay.
fieldNote: The **short warning** pushes him from calm to anxious despite his love of the tech.
He expects **shared hours** and half pay rather than a sacking, thanks to co-op rules.
He sees the three-year gap as time to **own the robots** together with other farms.

steps.text: Take the robot maintenance course straight away
Push a co-op vote on sharing hours fairly
Put an extra 150 a month into savings
Help other co-ops buy and own robots together

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this right: worker ownership, retraining, shorter weeks. At the Monday meeting I'd present a five-year plan. Online I'd share how small co-ops can club together to buy machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's much kinder to me. AGI in 2031 takes the office side when I'm 63, and robots in 2034 come when I'm 66 and about ready to stop anyway. The hours might thin out in my last year or two, but I can live with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the maintenance course over two winters instead of a crash course. I'd put a thousand into the co-op's machinery fund as a member share, so we can buy rather than rent the robots. And I'd keep saving, a hundred a month, as a buffer for those last thin years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Mostly fine for me, but things are moving around me and I'd be thinking about it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why put your own money into the machinery fund?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd rather own a slice of the farm robot than be replaced by someone else's. A thousand is a lot for us, but it's the same lesson as the warehouse. Whoever owns the machine keeps the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Neil think about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Neil thinks I'm mad, but a hopeful kind of mad. His portering job is hands-on too, so he's got the same few years. We've agreed we'd both rather stop at 66 with a little less than work till 70.

say: There's **time** to do this **right**: worker ownership, retraining and shorter weeks.
Small co-ops can **club together** to buy machines, and I'd share how.
think: With robots in **2034** I'm 66 and nearly ready to stop anyway.
My hours might **thin out** in the last year or two, which I can live with.
do: Do the **maintenance course** over two winters rather than as a crash course.
Put **a thousand** into the co-op's machinery fund as a member share.
Save **a hundred a month** as a buffer for the last thin years.
feel: **Uneasy**: mostly fine for me, but it would be on my mind every day.
S3.quote: I'd rather own a slice of the farm robot than be replaced by someone else's.
fieldNote: **Five years** of warning lets his retirement line up with the robot date.
Buying into the **machinery fund** is a real sacrifice from a modest cushion.
Neil's **portering job** faces the same robot timing, which they've planned around together.

steps.text: Do the robot maintenance course over two winters
Put 1,000 into the co-op machinery fund as a member share
Save 100 a month as a buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for leaving anyone behind. At the co-op I'd say let's be the farm other farms copy. Online I'd share what we're doing, warts and all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It barely touches my job. I'd be 68 when AGI comes and 71 when the robots do, so I'll have retired at 66. I'd get to enjoy the tools without the threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the rota and keep using AI every day to get better at pigs. I'd volunteer to run the co-op's AI planning before I go, so I leave something useful behind. And I'd vote and campaign for a shorter working week, because that's how you share the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, even. It's the version where I get the fun and somebody else gets the time to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you leave behind for the younger ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A records system that works and a co-op that owns its own robots, I hope. I'd like the young farmhand Jonah to be running the machines when I'm gone, not watching them from the dole queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still bother you in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the big farms would buy everything up while the small ones dithered. Ten years is plenty of time for the big money to get organised too.

say: **Ten years** is plenty, so there's no excuse for leaving anyone behind.
Long Acre should be **the farm** other farms copy, warts and all.
think: I'd be **retired at 66**, before AGI at 68 and robots at 71.
I get to enjoy the **tools** without the threat to my job.
do: Keep working the **rota** and use AI daily to get better with the pigs.
Set up the co-op's **AI planning** before I retire so I leave something useful.
Campaign for a **shorter working week** so the gains are shared.
feel: **Calm** and happy, getting the fun while others have time to plan.
S4.quote: I'd like the young farmhand Jonah to be running the machines when I'm gone, not watching them from the dole queue.
fieldNote: A decade of warning makes this the **easy version** for him personally.
His remaining worry is **big farms** buying up land faster than small ones organise.
He wants to leave a **working legacy**: records, owned robots and a trained successor.

steps.text: Keep working the Long Acre rota
Set up AI planning for the co-op before retiring
Campaign for a shorter working week

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd love the tools, but robots in 2031 would cut my hours before I'm ready to stop, and Neil's too. What would help is cheap loans for co-ops to buy their own robots, and a shorter working week so the work gets shared, not taken.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether people my age can learn this stuff. Everyone assumes we can't. I'm 58 and I talk to an AI every morning about pig worms. Anyone can learn this stuff if people stop assuming they can't.

headlineQuote: I'm 58 and I talk to an AI every morning about pig worms.
portrait: Adam is a **58-year-old** co-op member at Long Acre, two and a half years in after a robot warehouse made him redundant.
He uses **AI every day** and wants the co-op to own its robots, not be replaced by someone else's.
He stays calm in the slower scenarios but turns **anxious** in AGI by 2028, expecting shared hours and half pay.
His politics are about **sharing the gains**: worker ownership, shorter weeks and retraining.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots in 2031 would cut his and Neil's hours before **retirement**.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for co-ops to buy robots, and a **shorter week** so work is shared.
